abstract: AI use is spreading rapidly, but much less is known about businesses spending on AI. This column uses new survey evidence to estimate total AI spending in 2026 at around $280 billion in the US and $25 billion in the UK. Spending per employee is expected to increase by more than 40% in both countries compared with 2025, driven by younger, more productive, and higher-paying firms. Yet expenditure remains highly concentrated: fewer than 2% of firms account for half of total expected AI spending in each country.
authors: Ivan Yotzov, Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, Philip Bunn, Steven Davis, Kevin Foster, Aaron Jalca, Brent Meyer, Paul Mizen, Michael Navarrete, Gregory Thwaites
title: The concentration of AI spending

abstract: Should newly arrived refugee children immediately enter mainstream schools or first attend separated schools? Using the setting of the Netherlands, this column shows that the choice involves a major trade-off in the long run: direct integration reduces educational attainment, but it increases cultural assimilation as measured by hormonal-contraceptive use among teenage women. Separated schools’ greater access to teachers specialised in teaching the native language to non-native speakers offers a possible explanation for their educational advantage.
authors: Caterina Pavese, Simon ter Meulen, Ludger Woessmann
title: Schooling refugee children: Long-run effects of integration versus separation

abstract: Valuable shell resources may serve as a market-based governance mechanism by incentivizing firms to preserve shell value, thereby influencing corporate decisions. This paper examines whether and how shell resources affect real earnings management (REM). Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2018 and the implementation of the “Not Allowing Shell Listing on the Growth Enterprise Market (GEM)” policy as a quasi-natural experiment, we employ a difference-in-differences approach and find that shell resource depletion significantly increases REM among GEM firms. The results remain robust to a series of robustness tests. Mechanism analysis suggest that shell resource depletion increases REM by reducing firms’ disclosure quality. Further analyses show that the effect is more pronounced among firms with weaker internal control and higher industry competition. These findings highlight the governance consequences of shell resources and deepen our understanding of how capital-market institutions influence firms’ behavior.

title: Shell Resource Depletion and Real Earnings Management in Listed Companies: Evidence from China
